lines.raw: Chapter seven. The state space, and the Kalman filter.
lines.spoken: Chapter seven. The state space, and the Kalman filter.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> A state-space model has two equations. The state, which we cannot see, evolves linearly with Gaussian noise: a position and velocity, a river's underlying level, an economy's trend. <bookmark mark='b'/> We observe a linear function of it, plus noise. <bookmark mark='c'/> Before each observation, our belief about the state and the observation we expect are jointly Gaussian, assuming a Gaussian initial state and independent process and measurement noises. <bookmark mark='d'/> So after observing, the state's conditional distribution is Gaussian too, by the conditional-normal formula of Part five. The mean moves toward the observation by the gain K times the surprise, and the variance shrinks. That is the whole of the Kalman filter.
lines.spoken: A state-space model has two equations. The state, which we cannot see, evolves linearly with Gaussian noise: a position and velocity, a river's underlying level, an economy's trend. We observe a linear function of it, plus noise. Before each observation, our belief about the state and the observation we expect are jointly Gaussian, assuming a Gaussian initial state and independent process and measurement noises. So after observing, the state's conditional distribution is Gaussian too, by the conditional-normal formula of Part five. The mean moves toward the observation by the gain K times the surprise, and the variance shrinks. That is the whole of the Kalman filter.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Watch it as ellipses. A target moves with nearly constant velocity; we measure only its position, with noise. The state is two-dimensional: position across, velocity up. <bookmark mark='b'/> Each step, the prediction carries the last ellipse forward. Position moves by the velocity, so the ellipse shears and grows. <bookmark mark='c'/> The measurement says only where the position is, a vertical band; it says nothing directly about velocity. <bookmark mark='d'/> The update is the intersection, in the Gaussian sense: an ellipse narrower in position, and, because the predicted position and velocity were correlated, narrower in velocity too. Velocity is learned without ever being measured. <bookmark mark='e'/> Step after step, the ellipses settle into a steady size, tracking the true state in gold.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> In equations: predict the mean and covariance forward through the dynamics. <bookmark mark='b'/> Compare the observation with its prediction: the innovation, with its variance. <bookmark mark='c'/> Update by the gain. Rudolf Kálmán published the recursion in 1960; it needs only the last mean and covariance, not the whole history, which made it practical on the computers of the day. <bookmark mark='d'/> And an ignorable missing observation needs no measurement update: predict again, with greater uncertainty. Informative missingness requires modelling the observation process.

And an ignorable missing observation needs no measurement update: predict again, with greater uncertainty. Informative missingness requires modelling the observation process.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> For the local level the gain is the predicted variance over the predicted variance plus the noise variance. <bookmark mark='b'/> After a few steps it settles to a steady state, a fixed number determined by the ratio of the two variances. <bookmark mark='c'/> And then the filter's update is a weighted average of the new observation and the old level: Part seventeen's simple exponential smoothing, exactly. John Muth noticed this in 1960. <bookmark mark='d'/> For the Nile the signal-to-noise ratio of point zero nine seven gives a gain of point two seven. The state space explains why exponential smoothing works, and lets the likelihood choose its smoothing constant.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The Nile again, now its annual flow at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, the standard example of James Durbin and Siem Jan Koopman's textbook. The simplest state-space model, the local level, says the river has an underlying level that drifts as a random walk, and each year's flow is that level plus noise. <bookmark mark='b'/> Maximizing the likelihood gives a level variance of about fifteen hundred and a noise variance of about fifteen thousand: <bookmark mark='c'/> approximately the values in Durbin and Koopman's book, with a finite diffuse-prior approximation. <bookmark mark='d'/> The filtered level, in blue with its ninety percent band, follows the flows only slowly, discounting each year's surprise by the gain.
lines.spoken: The Nile again, now its annual flow at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, the standard example of James Durbin and Siem Jan Koopman's textbook. The simplest state-space model, the local level, says the river has an underlying level that drifts as a random walk, and each year's flow is that level plus noise. Maximizing the likelihood gives a level variance of about fifteen hundred and a noise variance of about fifteen thousand: approximately the values in Durbin and Koopman's book, with a finite diffuse-prior approximation. The filtered level, in blue with its ninety percent band, follows the flows only slowly, discounting each year's surprise by the gain.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Using all the data, past and future, gives the smoothed level, in green, the subject of chapter eight. <bookmark mark='b'/> Its biggest one-year fall comes into 1899. <bookmark mark='c'/> Adding a permanent shift at 1899 to the model, the likelihood picks a fall of about three hundred, and the likelihood improvement statistic of 10 point five is descriptive. The variances are held at their no-shift estimates, and the date was inspected in this same record, so this is not a calibrated likelihood-ratio test. <bookmark mark='d'/> Work on the first dam at Aswan began in 1898, and the climate of the basin became drier around the same time. This is evidence to investigate a level change, not causal attribution to the dam or a proof that the process broke.
